items: Define coupling and cohesion and explain why they predict maintainability.
Compute afferent/efferent coupling and instability (I = Ce / (Ca + Ce)).
Interpret cyclomatic complexity as a risk indicator for modules.
Describe the four DORA metrics and their elite/low performer bands.
Explain how fitness functions make quality measurable and continuous.
Afferent coupling (Ca) — number of external components that depend on a given component.
Efferent coupling (Ce) — number of external components a given component depends on.
Instability (I) — I = Ce / (Ca + Ce); ranges 0 (maximally stable) to 1 (maximally unstable).
Cohesion — degree to which elements within a module belong together.
Cyclomatic complexity — count of independent paths through code; higher means harder to test.
DORA metrics — Deployment Frequency, Lead Time for Changes, Change Failure Rate, MTTR.
Fitness function — an objective test that guards an architectural quality.

blocks.text: Coupling measures inter-dependencies. A module with high Ca is a "hub" — changing it risks many consumers, so it should be stable (low Ce). Instability I = Ce/(Ca+Ce) lets you balance the two: stable components (I near 0) should not depend on volatile ones. Cohesion is the counterpart: a highly cohesive module does one thing well, which lowers cognitive load and coupling. Low cohesion + high coupling is the classic recipe for a "big ball of mud."

Defined as M = E − N + 2P (edges − nodes + 2×connected components) on a control-flow graph. Practically, it equals decision points + 1. A method with complexity > 10 is a testing/risk hotspot; > 20 is a strong refactor candidate. Aggregated per service, it signals where defects concentrate.
The Accelerate / DORA research correlates four delivery metrics with organizational performance:

items: Deployment Frequency — how often you ship to production (elite: on-demand, multiple/day).
Lead Time for Changes — commit to production (elite: < 1 day).
Change Failure Rate — % of deployments causing failure (elite: 0–15%).
MTTR — time to restore service (elite: < 1 hour).

blocks.text: These quantify the "time to value" and "stability" trade-off better than vanity metrics like lines of code.

Coined in "Building Evolutionary Architectures," a fitness function is an automated check (test, static analysis, policy gate) that verifies a quality attribute continuously. Example: a test asserting that no service imports another service's internal package (coupling guard), or a pipeline step rejecting deploys that raise p99 latency.
